lesson.title: Subtracting Functions Cleanly: The Difference Rule
lesson.summary: The difference rule states that the derivative of f(x) minus g(x) equals f'(x) minus g'(x), following the same reasoning as the sum rule applied to subtraction.
lesson.body:
Subtraction is really just addition of a negative, and the difference rule for derivatives reflects that fact directly. If f and g are both differentiable, then the derivative of f(x) - g(x) is f'(x) - g'(x). This mirrors the sum rule covered previously so closely that it can be proven the same way, either by repeating the limit definition argument with a minus sign in place of a plus sign, or by treating f(x) - g(x) as f(x) + (-1) times g(x) and combining the sum rule with the constant multiple rule.

Working through the limit definition directly makes the parallel with the sum rule obvious. Let m(x) = f(x) - g(x). Then m(x+h) = f(x+h) - g(x+h), so the difference quotient is [m(x+h) - m(x)] / h = [f(x+h) - g(x+h) - f(x) + g(x)] / h. Regrouping by function, the numerator becomes [f(x+h) - f(x)] - [g(x+h) - g(x)], still divided by h, which splits into [f(x+h) - f(x)] / h minus [g(x+h) - g(x)] / h. Taking the limit as h approaches 0, and using the fact that the limit of a difference equals the difference of the limits, this becomes f'(x) - g'(x). So m'(x) = f'(x) - g'(x), exactly the claimed rule.

For a worked example, let f(x) = x^4 and g(x) = x^2, and consider m(x) = x^4 - x^2. By the power rule, f'(x) = 4x^3 and g'(x) = 2x. The difference rule then gives m'(x) = 4x^3 - 2x. Check this at x = 1: m'(1) = 4(1)^3 - 2(1) = 4 - 2 = 2. This matches computing each derivative separately at x = 1 and subtracting: f'(1) = 4(1)^3 = 4, g'(1) = 2(1) = 2, and 4 - 2 = 2, confirming the rule gives the correct number.

It is worth double checking this with the original function directly, at least conceptually: m(x) = x^4 - x^2, so m(1) = 1 - 1 = 0, and nearby values should reflect a slope of 2 at that point, meaning m is increasing at x = 1 at a moderate rate. The derivative rule saved the trouble of expanding (1+h)^4 and (1+h)^2 separately and combining them inside a single limit, which is precisely the time saving these rules exist to provide.

Between the sum rule and the difference rule, you now have full permission to differentiate any expression that adds or subtracts two or more differentiable pieces, term by term, in either direction. Combined with the constant multiple rule covered next, this sets up everything needed to differentiate an entire polynomial without ever touching the limit definition directly again.

It is natural to wonder whether the difference rule is really a separate fact or just the sum rule wearing a different name, since f(x) - g(x) can always be viewed as f(x) plus the negative of g(x). That intuition is correct in spirit, and once the constant multiple rule is available it gives a second, shorter proof of exactly the same result. For now, having a direct limit-based proof, independent of that later shortcut, is valuable on its own: it confirms the difference rule holds even before the constant multiple rule has been formally established, and it reinforces that subtraction of functions behaves every bit as predictably under differentiation as addition does.
